q.intro.text: Four stakes mark a garden bed. It looks like a square turned on its corner. Is it a square? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

q.cb.yes.text: You said yes. Its four sides do match, but its diagonals are twelve and ten: a rhombus with no right angle. Looking close is not the same as being equal.

q.cb.no.text: You said a rhombus, not a square. The numbers back you: four equal sides, but diagonals of twelve and ten, so no right angle.

q.cb.cant.text: You said you would need to measure the corners. You did not: the coordinates settled it exactly. Equal sides, unequal diagonals: a rhombus, not a square.

e.intro.text: One triangle, four tools. Every number comes from the coordinates, never from looking.

e.step0.text: Under A B sits a right triangle: run six, rise two. So A B squared is six squared plus two squared, forty. The same for B C: also forty. Equal squares, so the two sides are congruent.

e.step1.text: The slope of A B is one third; the slope of B C is negative three. Their product is negative one, so the sides are perpendicular: a right angle at B.

e.step2.text: The midpoint of A C is halfway in x and halfway in y: M is three, five, the average of the endpoints.

e.step3.text: M B squared is twenty, and M A squared is twenty too. B is as far from M as A is: B lies on the circle with diameter A C.

e.why.text: Why is A B squared equal to six squared plus two squared?

e.why.ok.text: Right: the run and the rise meet at a right angle, so the Pythagorean theorem gives the slanted side.

e.why.adds.text: The run and rise are not laid end to end along A B: they meet at a right angle. Square, add, take the root.

e.why.sq.text: Subtract first, then square: the legs are the differences, six and two.

t.intro.text: Your turn: P and Q. The run is eight and the rise is negative six.

t.pq.ok.text: Right: P Q squared is sixty-four plus thirty-six, a hundred, so P Q is ten.

t.pq.adds.text: The run and rise meet at a right angle: square them and add, do not add them.

t.pq.other.text: Square the run, square the rise, add, then take the square root.

t.m.ask.text: Now the midpoint M of P Q.

t.m.ok.text: Right: M is one, negative one, halfway in x and in y.

t.m.half.text: That is half the difference: how far M is from P. Add the coordinates, then halve.

t.m.other.text: Average each coordinate: add the two x values and halve, then the two y values.

t.s.ask.text: Last: the slope of a line perpendicular to P Q. Type it as a fraction.

t.s.ok.text: Right: P Q has slope negative three fourths, so a perpendicular has slope four thirds: the product is negative one.

t.s.recip.text: Flip and change the sign: the product of the slopes must be negative one.

t.s.opp.text: Change the sign and flip: the product of the slopes must be negative one.

t.s.other.text: First the slope of P Q: rise over run. Then flip it and change the sign.

t.done.text: That line through M is the perpendicular bisector of P Q. Now: can numbers like these prove a claim about every figure?

p.intro.text: Claim: the diagonals of every parallelogram bisect each other. First, place a general parallelogram on the axes.

p.place.ask.text: Which placement covers every parallelogram, and nothing more?

p.place.ok.text: Right: one side on the x-axis, the opposite side the same length and direction. Any parallelogram can be moved there.

p.place.rect.text: That builds in right angles: it covers rectangles only.

p.place.sq.text: That is a square: it proves the claim for squares only.

p.proved.text: Proved for every parallelogram: the letters stand for any one of them.

p.back.text: Back to the garden bed. Its four sides all have the same squared length. Is it a square?

p.back.ok.text: Right: A C is twelve but B D is ten. A rhombus with unequal diagonals has no right angle: not a square.

p.back.four.text: Four equal sides make a rhombus. A square also needs a right angle.

p.back.look.text: It looks close to square, but close is not equal: compute.
